# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
The comment's diagnostic work is valuable. It confirms several problems with the Halden paper from the microdata, and it adds a substantive correction to the record on attrition. The headline conclusion, however, is not supported by the comment's own analysis. After the authors' corrections, a gain of about 11% per actual hour remains. The argument that this residual is "entirely" novelty rests on an extrapolation from two survey points, a selective reading of the Varden trial, and a dismissal of the meetings hypothesis that holds that analysis to a standard the comment does not apply to itself.

## Arithmetic check

**Most figures are correct:**
- Table 2: 95.1/0.8 = +18.9%; 98.4/0.859 = +14.6%; 95.4/0.861 = +10.8%.
- Hours: 34.6/40.3 = −14.1%; 34.8/40.4 = −13.9%.
- Real revenue: 1.014/1.041 = −2.6%.
- Conclusion: "about four points" (3.8) and "about six points" (20 − 14.1) are both correct.

**Two figures don't hold:**
- **The hours components don't add up.** On a 32-hour schedule, longer days add +0.7 × 4 = 2.8 hours and day-off work adds 1.6 hours. That gives about 36.4 actual hours, not the reported 34.6. Measured against the baseline day of 40.3/5 ≈ 8.06 hours, the components give about 36.6. Either the components or the average is wrong. If actual hours were nearer 36.5, the per-hour gain would shrink further, so this matters for the comment's own case.
- **The novelty extrapolation is wrong.** Energy fell 0.32 SD between months three and six, about 0.107 per month. At that rate the remaining 0.29 SD reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten." The difference doesn't change the argument much, but the figure should be corrected.

## What the comment gets right

- **Attrition.** If the microdata show that seven of nine withdrawals came *after* the schedule began, and that six cited workload or output, the working paper's statement that they "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons" is materially inaccurate. The Halden authors should respond to this directly.
- **Output and hours.** The manager-versus-records comparison (19 of 23 organisations above their records) and the time-tracking data put numbers on the two biases the working paper only acknowledged.
- **Sector and revenue critiques.** The per-hour artifact in the sector table and the nominal-revenue problem are both correct. They are the same points I raised in my review of the working paper.
- **The Data note.** It is candid that the corrected subsets are non-random.

## 1. The abstract claims a correction that wasn't made

The abstract says "correcting the first three" problems (attrition, the output measure, hours) reduces the gain to 10.8%. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. Attrition is described in Section 1 but never corrected, and no figures exist for the withdrawers' output.

The abstract also says the four problems "account for most of the reported gain." Revenue plays no part in the per-hour calculation, so it can't account for any of it.

## 2. Attrition can't plausibly close the remaining gap

The comment implies that survivorship explains part of the residual, but a simple bound shows how little room there is:

- **If the nine withdrawers had zero per-hour gain:** weighting by organisation count, the gain becomes (61 × 10.8 + 9 × 0) / 70 ≈ 9.4%.
- **To pull the overall gain to zero:** the withdrawers would need an average per-hour change of about **−73%**, which is implausible.

Attrition is a fair objection to the working paper's framing. It is not a route to "entirely an artifact." A formal bounding analysis, such as worst-case or Lee bounds, would make this explicit.

## 3. The novelty argument is the weakest part, and it carries the conclusion

- **It uses the wrong variable.** The evidence is self-reported energy, not output. The comment never shows that *output per hour* declined over time.
- **The test it needs is already in the data.** The Halden output index was completed *monthly*, so the microdata contain an output time series. If the per-hour gain shrank from month 1 to month 6, that would be direct evidence of novelty. Its absence is the most important gap in the comment.
- **The extrapolation is thin.** Two post-baseline points (0.61, then 0.29) are compatible with a decline to zero, a plateau, or anything in between.
- **"The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter"** is a reasonable stance for withholding judgment. It does not support the positive claim that the gains *are* entirely artifactual. "Not shown to be durable" and "entirely an artifact" are different conclusions, and only the first is supported.

## 4. Selective use of the Varden trial

The comment calls Varden's counter-office result "the most reliable finding in the literature." It does not mention Varden's other registered result from the same design. In case-processing offices, output per *actual* hour rose **+12.5% (CI +6.9 to +18.4)**. That figure came from administrative records and timesheets, against a randomised control, at nine months.

This finding bears directly on the comment's argument:
- It is close to the comment's own corrected 10.8%.
- It excludes zero.
- It comes from a design without self-selection, manager reporting, or a scheduled-hours denominator.
- It was measured at nine months, past the comment's own projected fade point.

Control staff also knew a trial was running, which partly addresses Hawthorne-type effects. Varden's case-processing result is the strongest evidence *against* the "entirely an artifact" conclusion. A comment that relies on Varden for the negative finding needs to engage with it.

## 5. The meetings section mischaracterises Varden and applies a double standard

- **No subgroup was selected.** The seven offices were *all* treated case-processing offices, not a subgroup "selected for analysis after the results were known." What was unplanned was the meeting data collection, which the Varden authors disclosed.
- **Varden didn't claim a mechanism.** They called the finding exploratory, noted that seven offices "cannot establish a mechanism," and registered a confirmatory test. Saying it "should not be cited as a mechanism" restates their own caveat as if it were a rebuttal.
- **The standard isn't applied evenly.** The comment dismisses n = 7 here, yet relies on n = 3 retail organisations (the 11.2% fall) and a two-point extrapolation for its own claims.
- **The dismissal is doing work for the novelty argument.** If part of the gain comes from cutting low-value meetings, that is a structural change with no reason to fade. Dismissing the meetings hypothesis is what allows the residual to be attributed to novelty. As I noted in my review of Varden, its hours and meeting figures suggest meetings could account for most of the case-processing gain. That is unproven, but it is a live alternative to novelty, not something that can be set aside.

## 6. Scope

The Data note correctly says the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole." The conclusion then generalises to "the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes" in general, which is broader than the Halden pilot and contradicts the comment's own caveat. The repeated "in our assessment" softens the tone but doesn't resolve the logical gap.

## Minor points

- **Weighting.** Halden used employee-weighted means. The comment doesn't say how its subset means are weighted, so its 98.9, 98.4 and 95.4 figures may not be directly comparable with Halden's 98.7.
- **Records as a benchmark.** Records are better than manager ratings but are not ground truth. In professional services, "billable hours delivered" is partly an hours measure, which mechanically tracks the hours cut. Showing results by record type would help.
- **Revenue deflation.** CPI is a crude deflator for business revenue, since sector output prices differ. The direction of the correction is right, but the size is approximate.

## Overall

The comment supports a strong, useful conclusion:

> The Halden headline of +23.4% is roughly halved by record-based output and actual hours. Attrition was misreported. Sector-generality is unsupported. Durability is unproven. In presence-bound work, reduced hours reduce output.

It does not support "entirely an artifact." With the Varden case-processing result, the evidence currently points to a real but much smaller per-hour gain, roughly 10–12%, in backlog-type work. Whether that gain is durable is open. Its source, rest or the removal of low-value time, is also open, and the answer matters for whether it would fade. The comment would be considerably stronger if it ran the monthly output-per-hour trend from the microdata, bounded attrition formally, and engaged with Varden's case-processing result.
